units.summary: A man who broke a borrowed ax is told by Rav to replace it with a new one, but Rav's colleagues challenge the ruling and Rav concedes through silence.
After Rav Naḥman leaves the room, Ulla clarifies a legal ruling of Rabbi Elazar to the remaining students.
Judges in Neharde’a and Pumbedita collected slaves from orphans to pay debts, but Rav Naḥman ordered them to return the property.
The Gemara describes the unique funeral honors given to King Hezekiah, including a massive procession and the placement of a Torah scroll on his bier.
Rabba bar bar Hana describes his habit of following Rabbi Yohanan to ask questions and how the Rabbi would only answer after performing his post-lavatory rituals.
A donkey ate bread and broke the basket it was in, leading Rav Yehuda to rule that the owner must pay full damages for the bread and half for the basket.
A goat climbed a clay barrel to eat a turnip, breaking the barrel in the process, leading Rava to rule that the owner must pay full damages for both.
Rav Hisda tells Rami bar Hama about a legal dilemma regarding a squatter that was discussed in the academy while Rami bar Hama was absent.
Rabbi Abbahu misinterprets Rabbi Yohanan's silence as agreement with his legal conclusion, leading him to cite it in Yohanan's name.
Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sends a legal query to Rav Huna, but Rav Huna passes away before answering, leading his son Rabba to provide the ruling in his stead.
A man built a mansion on land belonging to orphans, and Rav Nahman confiscated the building from him.
Rav Yosef asks Abaye to warn the Tarbu family about their damaging goats, but Abaye refuses, arguing that the burden of fencing lies with the victim.
The Gemara cites two incidents in Neharde’a and Pumbedita where pedestrians broke jugs and were held liable by Shmuel and Rava.
A man caught his partner drawing water from their shared cistern out of turn and struck him with a hoe, an act Rav Naḥman later justified.
Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahava penalized people who left barley in the public domain by declaring their property ownerless.
Rav Huna declared a group's barley ownerless after they were warned to remove it from the public domain and refused to comply.
Rava slaps Rav Shimi's sandal as a gesture of disparagement while refuting his legal explanation regarding the administration of lashes.
Rav Taḥalifa recites a baraita concerning the sale or consecration of a goring ox in the presence of Rabbi Abbahu.
Rabbi Abbahu recites a baraita before Rabbi Yoḥanan, who rejects the teaching and tells him to go teach it outside the study hall.
An ox belonging to Rav Pappa had a toothache, broke into a vessel of beer, drank it, and was healed.

A man who was slapped initially refuses a small fine and directs it to the poor, but when he tries to retract his donation, Rav Yosef rules that the court has already acquired it on behalf of the poor.
Ḥanan the wicked slaps a man and is ordered by Rav Huna to pay a half-dinar fine, but he only possesses a clipped full dinar and cannot find change.

The Roman government sends two officials to study Torah with the Sages, and after thorough study, they praise the Torah's truth while noting a legal discrepancy regarding damages caused by gentiles' oxen.

After the death of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's daughter, Ulla refuses to join the Sages in their standard Babylonian consolation and instead visits alone to offer a teaching about God's foresight. Ulla visits the mourning Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda and consoles him by explaining that God spares nations only for the sake of future righteous descendants, implying his daughter lacked such potential.
Rava praises Rav Aha bar Ya'akov to Rav Nahman, but when they meet, Rav Aha's questions are so difficult that Rav Nahman asks him to stop.
Shimon HaAmasoni, who systematically interpreted the word 'et' in the Torah, abandoned his project when he reached the command to fear God, until Rabbi Akiva later resolved the difficulty.
Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva debate the derivation of ransom payments for an ox that kills.
Rav Haggai arrives from the South bringing a baraita that supports Rav Adda bar Ahava's legal interpretation.
Rav Dimi arrives from Eretz Yisrael to report Rabbi Yoḥanan's view on ransom, leading to a verbal challenge from Abaye.
Ravin arrives from Eretz Yisrael and reports a legal tradition from Rabbi Yoḥanan regarding slaves.
Rav and Shmuel debate the legal status of a sale where an ox is found to be a gorer, focusing on whether the transaction is a mistake based on the majority of buyers' intentions.
A woman entered a house to bake, the homeowner's goat ate her dough and died, and Rava held her liable for the damages.
When the daughter of Neḥunya the ditchdigger falls into a deep cistern, Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa monitors her status through prayer until she is miraculously rescued by a ram led by an old man.
Despite Neḥunya's dedication to providing water for the public, his own son died of thirst, illustrating God's strictness with the righteous.
A man ignores a pious man's warning about throwing stones from his field into public property, only to later sell the field and trip over those same stones while walking in the public domain.

An ox falls into a shallow channel and the owner slaughters it immediately out of fear it will die, but Rav Nachman rules the meat forbidden because the owner did not wait to see if it would survive the impact.
Rav Nahman rules that an ox which fell into a shallow water channel and was immediately slaughtered is forbidden as a tereifa due to the impact of the fall.
Rabbi Ḥanina ben Agil, unable to get an answer from Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba regarding the Ten Commandments, travels to Rabbi Tanḥum who provides a tradition on the matter.
The Gemara discusses the legal liability of one who stands in front of an animal to direct it into a neighbor's field.
A man cut down another's date palm and was brought before the Exilarch, who ordered him to pay one hundred zuz based on his own knowledge of the tree's value.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua rule on the method of appraising a damaged date palm.

Eliezer Ze’eira is questioned by the Exilarch's officials for wearing black shoes and proves his scholarly status through a legal challenge. Eliezer Ze’eira is questioned by the Exilarch's officials for wearing black shoes in mourning, proves his scholarly status by answering a difficult legal question about date palms, and is vindicated by Shmuel.
Upon hearing that the righteous are the first to perish in a plague, Rav Yosef weeps, and Abaye comforts him by explaining it is a kindness to spare them from seeing the coming evil.
During a plague, Rava would close his windows to protect himself.
Rav Ami and Rav Asi pull Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa in different directions regarding his teaching, leading him to compare himself to a man with two wives who pluck out all his hair.
The Gemara interprets the biblical story of David and the water from Bethlehem as a series of legal inquiries regarding damages.
A man kicks another's safe into a river, leading the owner to claim it contained a pearl, which Rav Ashi then deliberates upon without reaching a final decision.
Rava notes that Rabba posed a legal difficulty to Rav Yosef for twenty-two years until Rav Yosef became head of the academy and resolved it.
Rava questions Rav Naḥman about a thief's liability for a shared animal, leading Rav Naḥman to rule one way in the evening and retract his position the following morning.
Rav Yirmeya of Difti reports that Rav Pappa once ruled according to Rava's view on conspiring witnesses, while Rav Ashi asserts the halakha follows Abaye.
Rabban Gamliel blinds his slave Tavi and joyfully tells Rabbi Yehoshua that the slave is now free, only to be told that his self-admission without witnesses is legally insufficient to grant freedom.
A pious man is prescribed goat's milk for his heart condition, but his friends shun him for keeping a goat in his house, leading him to confess this as his only sin before he dies.
Rabbi Yishmael recounts how his family's wealth in the Galilee was lost because they grazed animals improperly and judged cases individually.
An unmarried woman impulsively swears to marry anyone who will discipline her son, but the Sages intervene to dissolve the oath when unworthy men try to hold her to it.
After Rav Huna justifies keeping sheep by saying his wife Hova watches them, Rav Adda bar Ahava curses her, resulting in the death of Rav Huna's children.

Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Asi arrive at a celebration, leading to a dilemma over the order in which they should enter the house. While Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Asi are politely debating who should enter a celebration first, a cat mauls a baby, prompting Rav to issue a harsh ruling against keeping cats.
While walking with Rav Yehuda, Shmuel veers off the main road to avoid obstacles, demonstrating the practical application of Joshua's stipulations.

While walking, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya observe Rabbi Yehuda ben Kanosa refusing to veer off the road; Rabbi Hiyya explains his student's pious motivations, leading to a respectful encounter.
The prophets instituted the regular Monday and Thursday Torah readings after the Israelites became exhausted from traveling three days in the desert without the 'water' of Torah.
During the Hasmonean civil war, a Greek-wise elder advises the besiegers of Jerusalem to send up a pig instead of sacrificial animals, leading to a national catastrophe and subsequent rabbinic bans.
During the Hasmonean civil war, a Greek-wise elder advises the besiegers to send a pig instead of a sheep, leading to a miraculous earthquake and a rabbinic curse on raising pigs.
A woman enters a house to bake and is so frightened by a barking dog that she miscarries, despite the owner's claims that the dog is harmless.
A donkey severs a child's hand, but the father refuses a court appraisal of the child's value as a slave, opting to compensate the child himself when he grows up.
An ox injures a child's hand, and when Rava orders an appraisal, the court officers challenge him based on his own jurisdictional rules.
The Gemara mentions that Rav Pappa once collected four hundred zuz as compensation for humiliation.
Rabba recounts finding the Sages in Rav's study hall debating the rationale behind Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on medical bandages.
Rav Yosef describes how his perspective on his own blindness and religious obligation shifted after hearing a teaching by Rabbi Hanina, changing his criteria for hosting a celebratory feast.

The mother of Rav Shmuel bar Abba married Rabbi Abba and subsequently transferred her property to her son. Rav Shmuel bar Abba successfully claims his mother's property before Rabbi Yirmeya, but his stepfather Rabbi Abba challenges the ruling before other sages, leading to a legal reversal.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna arrive from the study hall and cite a Mishnaic proof for the ordinance of Usha.
A man who was fined for uncovering a woman's head tries to trick her into uncovering it herself to prove she isn't easily humiliated, but Rabbi Akiva maintains the fine.
A man strikes another and Rabbi Yehuda Nesia rules that he must pay a Tyrian maneh in accordance with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
A man who humiliated a woman by uncovering her head in public tries to avoid paying the fine by tricking her into uncovering her own head in public, but Rabbi Akiva maintains the penalty.
Rabban Gamliel fined a man ten gold coins for preemptively covering the blood of an animal slaughtered by someone else, thereby stealing the original slaughterer's mitzvah.
Rabbi Hanina attributes the untimely death of his son, Shivhat, to the fact that he cut down a fruit-bearing fig tree.
Shmuel tastes wine in dates brought by his sharecropper and, upon learning the palms grow among vines, orders them cut down to protect the more valuable grapes.
Rav Hisda sees date palms among his grapevines and instructs his sharecropper to uproot them because vines are more valuable.
Moses prays for Judah's bones to stop rolling in their coffin and for Judah to be admitted to the heavenly academy.
Rav Yosef deposits a charity purse with a man who is negligent, leading to its theft and a subsequent ruling of liability.

A long-time thief attempts to repent, but his wife discourages him by pointing out that he will be left with nothing if he returns all his stolen goods, leading the Sages to institute an ordinance protecting penitents.
A man steals oxen to plow his field and returns them, leading Rav Nahman to rule that he must pay the victim for the enhancement the oxen provided to his land, despite Rava's objections.
The household of Rav Yosef bar Ḥama used to seize the slaves of debtors to work them, leading to a confrontation where his son Rabba challenged the practice as appearing like forbidden interest.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua presided over a case involving the exchange of Agardemis coins at a specific rate.
Ameimar rules on the liability of someone who burned another person's promissory note.
Rav Hisda encounters Rabba bar Shmuel and asks him if he has learned a baraita regarding returning stolen items.
A man brings a slaughtered animal to Rav, who declares it non-kosher and exempts the butcher, leading Rav Kahana and Rav Asi to later comment to the man on the nature of the ruling.
A woman relies on Rabbi Hiyya's validation of a coin, but when it is later rejected by others, Hiyya instructs that she be compensated from his own funds.
Reish Lakish shows a coin to Rabbi Elazar for assessment and warns him that he is relying on his expert opinion, leading to a discussion on liability.
While sitting in a lesson, Rav Yosef physically turns his face away in disdain when Rav Huna issues a ruling he considers redundant.
Rav Kahana purchased flax that remained with the seller, and after it increased in value and was sold by the seller, Rav ruled on Rav Kahana's right to the profits.
A pious man who forgot which of two people he bought an item from seeks guidance from Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva on how to properly pay his debt.

Rabbi Abba sends Rav Safra to collect a debt from Rav Yosef bar Ḥama, but Rava advises the debtor not to pay because a receipt from the agent wouldn't protect him if Rabbi Abba died before the agent returned.
Rav Pappa transfers a large debt to Rav Shmuel bar Abba using a legal loophole involving land, and later goes out to meet him upon his return.
Rav Nahman sits and teaches a law, and Rav Aha bar Minyumi and Rami bar Hama challenge him with objections from a Mishna.
Rav Gamda travels to Rav Ashi to report a legal tradition, which Rav Ashi and Rav Aha the Elder then discuss.
Rabbi Yirmeya's young brother-in-law physically locks him out of a house to protect his inheritance, leading to a court case where Rabbi Avin rules in the minor's favor.
Rabbi Yirmeya's minor brother-in-law locks him out of a house, leading to a legal dispute that travels from Rabbi Avin to Rabbi Abbahu regarding testimony against minors.
Ravina delayed a legal authorization for twelve months because the creditor was a violent man who would not return property even if the claim was later overturned.
Rav Asi visits Rav Kahana and observes him immediately ostracizing a woman for missing a single court summons, leading to a discussion on why the standard grace period for men does not apply to her.
Shmuel takes advantage of a gentile's error by purchasing a gold bowl at the price of an iron one, adding a single coin to the payment.
Rav Kahana and Ravina engage in transactions with gentiles where they benefit from the gentiles' counting errors.
While traveling, Rav Ashi tells his servant to take grapes if they belong to a gentile, but the servant points out that robbing a gentile is also prohibited.
A man's offhand childhood memories of being called a priest-specific nickname lead Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to formally recognize his priestly status.
An incident involving a woman's eligibility for marriage comes before the sages, resulting in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permitting her to marry a priest.
Hanan the Wicked stole and sold a cloak, and Rav Huna ruled that the owner must reimburse the purchaser because the thief was insolvent.
Avimi bar Nazi accepted a stolen cloak as repayment for an old debt and then lent more money; Ravina later ruled on how much the original owner must pay to retrieve it.
A thief from Naresh sold a stolen scroll which was then resold at a profit; Abaye and Rava debated and ruled on how the original owner and the various purchasers should settle the costs.
While traveling in a caravan followed by a lion, Rav Safra offers his donkey as the nightly sacrifice, but the lion does not eat it, allowing Rav Safra to reclaim it the next morning.
A man informs thugs about the Exilarch's wheat, leading to its seizure and a subsequent ruling by Rav Nachman that the informant must pay for the loss.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda reports a ruling he made regarding an informer to Rava, who orders him to reverse the decision and return the money.
A man is coerced into showing and carrying Rav Mari's wine for thugs, and Rav Ashi exempts him from liability.
Two people quarrel over a net and one gives it to a king's officer, leading to Abaye's ruling.

After killing an informer and fleeing to Eretz Yisrael on Rav's advice, Rav Kahana's intellectual prowess inadvertently offends Rabbi Yoḥanan, leading to Rav Kahana's death. Rabbi Yoḥanan travels to the burial cave of Rav Kahana, convinces a mystical serpent to let him enter, and resurrects Rav Kahana after realizing he had caused his death through a misunderstanding.
After an informer causes Rabbi Abba's silk to be seized by gentiles, Rabbi Abba seeks a ruling from various sages until he finds a court that holds the informer liable.
A man gives a deposited silver cup to thieves to save himself, and Rabba rules that he is exempt from reimbursing the owner.
A man entrusted with funds for redeeming captives gives the money to thieves to save himself, and Rava rules he is not liable.
On a ferry, a man pushes another's donkey into the water to prevent the boat from sinking, leading to a legal discussion on liability.
Rava purchases grapevine branches from a sharecropper and defends the legality of the act when challenged by Abaye.
Rav Hisda dismisses his sharecropper for being overly precise in weighing produce, suspecting him of theft.
When Ravina visits Bei Mehoza, the local women donate expensive jewelry to him for charity, leading to a discussion on whether such large gifts may be accepted from women.
Rav Yehuda mentions that his son Yitzḥak was personally strict and would not take certain threads for himself.
